entry: Handled bag used to carry personal items. Also called a purse in North American English and a pocketbook in parts of the U.S., it was carried in antiquity: Egyptian burial sites (c. 2686–2160 BC) have yielded [[Leather|leather]] bags with two straps. The [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greeks]] used leather, papyrus and linen purses called *byrsa*, the origin of the English word "purse". The Courtauld bag, tentatively believed to have been made at [[Mosul]] in the early 1300s, is thought to be the oldest surviving handbag and likely belonged to an [[Ilkhanate]] noblewoman. In late 18th-century Europe, fashion favored slender reticules carried on wrist straps, while men kept purses and pockets. The modern handbag took shape in England during the [[Industrial Revolution]], partly through rail travel.

Indoor team sport played by two teams of seven players each, six outfield players and a goalkeeper. Players pass the ball by hand and throw it into the opposing goal, and only the defending goalkeeper may enter the 6 m zone around each goal. A standard match has two 30-minute periods on a 40 by 20 m court. The modern rules were published on October 29, 1917, by Karl Schelenz, Max Heiser and Erich Konigh in [[Berlin]], a date seen as the sport's birth. Men's handball was first played at the Olympics in Berlin in 1936, outdoors, and at [[Munich]] in 1972, indoors; women's handball was added in 1976. European countries have won all but one of the medals in the men's Olympic tournament since 1972, and the sport is also popular in East Asia, North Africa and parts of South America.

[[Firearm]] designed to be held and fired with one hand. Handguns have shorter effective ranges than long guns, lack stocks and are much harder to shoot accurately. Early handguns were mostly single-shot [[Pistol|pistols]]; after mass production of the Colt Paterson began in 1836, most handguns became [[Revolver|revolvers]] or semi-automatic pistols. Before mass production, a handgun was often a badge of office, comparable to a ceremonial [[Sword|sword]]. Samuel Colt patented the Colt Paterson, the first practical mass-produced revolver, which fired five shots in rapid succession. Handguns came to be defined as weapons for personal defense and are used mostly as sidearms by law enforcement. Firearms began in [[China]], and the Heilongjiang hand cannon of 1288 is the oldest known bronze barrel handgun. In 1432 the [[Joseon]] dynasty under [[Sejong the Great]] introduced the se-chongtong.

Item production entirely by hand or with simple tools. Handicraft covers creative work with textiles, clay, wood, metal, paper and plant fibers, usually in traditional techniques that produce items both practical and aesthetic. Handicraft industries make goods for local needs without machines, and the individual artisanship of each item is the key criterion, so mass-produced goods do not qualify. Many crafts have been practiced for centuries. One of the oldest is Dhokra, a metal casting practiced in [[India]] for over 5,000 years. Handicrafts often carry cultural or religious meaning and may carry political messages, as in craftivism. The [[Arts and Crafts movement]], a late-19th-century design reform and social movement, drew on the belief that pre-industrial people found fulfillment through handicrafts. The [[Industrial Revolution]] and increasing [[Mechanization|mechanization]] reduced the roles of professional craftspeople, and many handicrafts are now practiced as hobbies or folk art.

Manual stimulation of a penis by a sex partner. A handjob is a sexual act in which a person stimulates the penis or scrotum by hand to induce an erection, arousal and possibly orgasm. It may be [[Foreplay|foreplay]] or [[Non-penetrative sex|non-penetrative sex]], and it is analogous to fingering. Some people choose it to avoid the risks of penetrative sex, such as [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]] and pregnancy, or to preserve virginity. A 2011 investigation by *Time Out New York* found that many [[New York City]] massage parlors advertised handjobs.

Japanese international airport, the busier of two serving the Greater Tokyo Area. Located in Ōta, 15 km south of Tokyo Station, it is the primary domestic base of Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways. Haneda was the main international airport serving Tokyo until 1978. A dedicated international terminal opened in 2010, and daytime long-haul service began in March 2014. It handled 87,098,683 passengers in 2018, the third-busiest airport in Asia. In 2020 it was named the second-best airport after [[Changi Airport]], and it held second place in Skytrax's world top 100 airports in 2021 and 2022.

Method of killing by suspension from the neck with a noose or ligature. Hanging has been a standard method of [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]] since the [[Middle Ages]] and the primary execution method in many countries. The first known account of execution by hanging appears in [[Homer|Homer]]'s *Odyssey*. Before 1850 the short drop was the standard method, and death came by strangulation. From 1866 the standard drop, of 1.2–1.8 m, was considered more humane and spread through English-speaking countries after Irish doctor Samuel Haughton published its scientific details. Hanging is also a common method of [[Suicide|suicide]].

Alphabetic writing system of the Korean language. Called Chosŏn'gŭl in North Korea and Hangeul in South Korea, the script was created under [[Sejong the Great]] of the [[Joseon]] dynasty and published in 1446 in the text *Hunminjeongeum*. Korea had used [[Chinese characters|Hanja]] since antiquity, but Hanja was poorly suited to Korean, and its difficulty contributed to widespread illiteracy. The elite looked down on Hangul for centuries, and it gained wide acceptance only in the late 19th century. It is now the predominant script for Korean in both Koreas and among the Korean diaspora. Modern orthographies use 24 basic letters called jamo, 14 consonants and 10 vowels. Combinations yield 27 more letters, for 51 in total, arranged in syllable blocks. Linguists and historians have praised the script.

Capital and most populous city of [[Zhejiang]] Province, China. Hangzhou lies at the southern end of the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]], near the head of Hangzhou Bay, and is known for its cultural heritage and [[West Lake]]. In the Tang dynasty the poet [[Bai Juyi]], as governor, ordered a stronger dyke and a dam to control the lake's water, relieving drought. In 1089 [[Su Shi]] used 200,000 workers to build a 2.8 km causeway across West Lake. The city served as the capital of the Wuyue Kingdom and later of the [[Song dynasty|Southern Song dynasty]]. Hangzhou has three [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]]: the West Lake Cultural Landscape, the Grand Canal and the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City. It hosts the headquarters of [[Alibaba Group]], Ant Group, DeepSeek, Geely and NetEase.

American country singer and songwriter. Born Hiram Williams in Alabama, he learned guitar from a [[Blues|blues]] musician, Rufus Payne, and became an early pioneer of [[Country music|country music]]. Because [[Alcoholism|alcoholism]] made him unreliable, he was repeatedly fired and rehired by one radio station. His single "Move It On Over" was a hit in 1947, and his cover of "Lovesick Blues" reached number one on Billboard's country chart and made him a star on the Grand Ole Opry. He wrote "Your Cheatin' Heart", "Hey, Good Lookin'" and "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry", although he was unable to read or notate music to any significant degree. Of his 55 singles to reach the country top 10, 12 reached No. 1. In 2010 he was posthumously awarded a [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prize]] special citation. [[Elvis Presley]] and [[Bob Dylan]] were among the artists he influenced.

American animation studio, active from 1957 to 2001. Founded in Los Angeles by William Hanna and Joseph Barbera, former MGM cartoon makers who had created *Tom and Jerry*, the studio pioneered cost-effective limited animation for television. Its series included *Huckleberry Hound*, *The Flintstones*, *Yogi Bear*, *Jonny Quest*, *Scooby-Doo* and *The Smurfs*. Taft Broadcasting owned the studio before Turner Broadcasting System bought it in 1991 and used its back catalog to help launch [[Cartoon Network]] in 1992. The studio was absorbed into Warner Bros. Animation in 2001.

German-American political theorist and philosopher. Arendt is best known for her work on wealth, power, [[Totalitarianism|totalitarianism]] and evil, and for the phrase "the banality of evil", associated with her reporting on the trial of [[Adolf Eichmann]]. She studied at Marburg under [[Martin Heidegger]] and was briefly imprisoned by the [[Gestapo]] in 1933 for research into [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]]. After leaving Germany she spent years in Paris and reached the United States in 1941. *The Origins of Totalitarianism* (1951) established her reputation, followed by *The Human Condition* (1958) and *Eichmann in Jerusalem* (1963). She taught at many American universities while declining tenure-track appointments.

Carthaginian general and statesman. Hannibal commanded the forces of [[Carthage]] against the [[Roman Republic]] in the Second Punic War, which began in 218 BC when he attacked Saguntum, an ally of Rome in Hispania. He crossed the [[Alps]] with war elephants and won a series of victories in Italy, including at [[Battle of Cannae|Cannae]], but was unable to win a decisive victory after Carthaginian defeats in Hispania prevented reinforcement. He held most of southern Italy for about 15 years. Defeated at Zama by the Roman general [[Scipio Africanus]], he returned to Carthage. He later enacted financial reforms to pay Rome's war indemnity, then went into exile and served [[Antiochus III the Great]] against Rome. Betrayed to the Romans, he poisoned himself.

Fictional character created by American novelist Thomas Harris. Lecter, a cannibalistic [[Serial killer|serial killer]] and former forensic psychiatrist, first appeared as a minor villain in Harris's 1981 novel *Red Dragon*. He had a larger role in *The Silence of the Lambs* (1988). [[Anthony Hopkins]] played him in the 1991 film, for which Hopkins won the Academy Award for Best Actor. Mads Mikkelsen played Lecter in the NBC series *Hannibal* (2013–2015). In 2003 the American Film Institute named Hopkins's portrayal the greatest villain in American cinema. Harris drew partial inspiration from a Mexican prison doctor who was in fact a convicted murderer.

Carthaginian explorer of the 5th century BC. Hanno led a naval expedition of 60 ships and 30,000 people along the western coast of Africa, founding cities as it went. His account, the *Periplus*, is one of the few surviving accounts of ancient exploration written by its leader, though only Greek abridgements survive of the lost Punic original. The account describes meeting the Lixitae, passing fires and a very tall mountain, and killing three [[Gorilla|gorillas]], whose skins were brought back to Carthage. It ends without describing the return. Historians debate the route: some analyses suggest it reached as far south as [[Gabon]], while others argue it could not have sailed much beyond southern [[Morocco]]. Some historians question the account's accuracy because of its hyperbolic distances and dramatic elements.

[[Capital city|Capital]] and second-most populous city of [[Vietnam]] (pop., 2023: 8,587,141). Hanoi covers 3,358.6 sq km and houses the National Assembly and the presidential palace. Founded in 1010 by the Lý dynasty emperor Lý Thái Tổ as Thăng Long, it was renamed Đông Kinh in 1428 and became Hanoi in 1831. It was the capital of [[French Indochina]] from 1902 to 1945 and became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam in 1976. Sites include the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the [[Ho Chi Minh]] Mausoleum and Hoàn Kiếm Lake. [[UNESCO]] designated Hanoi a City of Peace in 1999.

Capital and largest city of the German state of [[Lower Saxony]] (pop., 2021: 535,932). Hanover was the seat of the Hanoverian kings of the [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland|United Kingdom]] by personal union from 1714 to 1837. Before 1946 it had been capital of several Hanoverian and Prussian states. It is a major rail and motorway crossing, and its fairground, enlarged for Expo 2000, is the largest in the world. The city hosts the Hanover Fair and the biannual IAA Commercial Vehicles show, and in 2014 it was named a [[UNESCO]] City of Music.

German-American physicist. Bethe made major contributions to [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physics]], astrophysics, [[Quantum electrodynamics|quantum electrodynamics]] and solid-state physics. His 1939 paper established the CNO cycle as the main energy source of heavier stars on the main sequence, which earned him the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1931 he developed the Bethe ansatz, a method for exact solutions of certain one-dimensional quantum many-body models. During World War II he headed the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos, part of the [[Manhattan Project]], where he helped calculate critical mass and develop the implosion method used in the [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity test]]. After the war he played a role in developing the hydrogen bomb, then campaigned with [[Albert Einstein]] against nuclear testing and the [[Nuclear arms race|nuclear arms race]]. His 1947 calculation of the Lamb shift is credited with revolutionizing quantum electrodynamics. He spent most of his career at [[Cornell University]].

Danish writer best remembered for his literary [[Fairy tale|fairy tales]]. Andersen also wrote plays, travelogues, novels and poems, but his fairy tales, 156 stories across nine volumes, have been translated into more than 125 languages. Among the best known are "The Emperor's New Clothes", "The Little Mermaid", "The Nightingale", "The Ugly Duckling" and "Thumbelina". At 14 he moved to [[Copenhagen]] to seek work as an actor. He was accepted into the Royal Danish Theatre, but his voice soon changed, and a colleague's suggestion led him to focus on writing. His stories have inspired ballets, plays, and animated and live-action films.

Danish chemist and physicist. In 1820 Ørsted showed that an electric current deflects a compass needle, demonstrating that electric currents produce magnetic fields; this relationship is known as Oersted's law. He had been investigating the connection since 1818, and the story that he found it by chance during a lecture is a myth. The finding spurred research by [[André-Marie Ampère|André-Marie Ampère]] and [[Michael Faraday|Michael Faraday]]. Ørsted became a professor at the [[University of Copenhagen]] in 1806 and in 1819 was the first to extract piperine from black pepper. He also discovered aluminum. A leader of the Danish Golden Age, he was a close friend of [[Hans Christian Andersen]].

German painter and printmaker active in Switzerland and England. Holbein worked in a Northern Renaissance style and is considered one of the greatest portraitists of the 16th century. Born in Augsburg, he worked mainly in [[Basel]], where he produced religious works, woodcuts and book illustrations, and made his name with portraits of [[Erasmus|Desiderius Erasmus]]. He traveled to England in 1526 on Erasmus's recommendation and joined the humanist circle of [[Thomas More]]. After four years in Basel, he resumed his career in England in 1532 under Anne Boleyn and [[Thomas Cromwell]]. By 1535 he was King's Painter to [[Henry VIII]], producing portraits of the royal family and nobles, as well as designs for jewelry and plate. Holbein founded no school, but his portraits were prized for their likeness and symbolism, and art historian Ellis Waterhouse called them "unsurpassed" for their sureness and economy of statement.

German-born British biochemist. Krebs was a pioneer in the study of [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]], the process by which cells extract energy from food and oxygen. With Kurt Henseleit, he discovered the urea cycle, the metabolic pathway for urea formation, while at Freiburg in 1932. He is best known for the [[Citric acid cycle|citric acid cycle]], often called the Krebs cycle, which lets oxygen-respiring cells obtain far more ATP from food than [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]] can supply. That work earned him the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Nazi racial laws ended his career in Germany, and he settled in England, working at [[Oxford]] from 1954 until his retirement in 1967. He was knighted in 1958.

German film composer and music producer. Zimmer has composed music for more than 150 films since the 1980s, integrating electronic sounds with traditional orchestral arrangements. He has twice won the Academy Award for Best Original Score, for *The Lion King* (1994) and *Dune* (2021). His scores include *Gladiator*, the *Pirates of the Caribbean* series and *Inception*. He has worked with director [[Christopher Nolan]] on six films, from *Batman Begins* to *Dunkirk*. He co-founded Remote Control Productions and heads the film music division at DreamWorks.

Medieval commercial and defensive network of merchant [[Guild|guilds]] and market towns. Known as the Hansa, it grew from Lübeck and other North German towns in the late 12th century and eventually encompassed nearly 200 settlements in eight modern-day countries, from [[Estonia]] and Russia to the [[Netherlands]]. The league dominated maritime trade in the North and Baltic Seas through trading posts, or kontors, in [[London]] (the Steelyard), [[Bruges]], Bergen and Novgorod. It could impose blockades and wage war on kingdoms, yet it lacked a permanent administrative body, a treasury or a standing army. Its only autonomous landed member was the [[Teutonic Order]]. The league gradually unraveled from the mid-16th century and disintegrated in 1669.

German [[Fairy tale|fairy tale]] collected by the [[Brothers Grimm]]. Siblings are abandoned in a forest and find a witch's house made of bread, cake and sugar. The witch plans to fatten Hansel before eating him, but Gretel pushes her into her own oven, and the children escape with the witch's treasure. The tale was published in 1812 as part of *Grimms' Fairy Tales*. The Grimms credited tales from [[Hesse]], but scholars argue they heard the story from the family of Wilhelm Grimm's future wife. In later editions the mother became a stepmother. Engelbert Humperdinck's opera *Hänsel und Gretel* was first performed in 1893.
